title: App Deployment
summary: Build in a sandbox, test, then move it safely: sandboxes, change sets, packages and a release plan that never surprises your users.

lessons.title: The life of a change
lessons.objective: Given a set of business requirements, recommend a solution for managing the application lifecycle, including sandbox types.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: The **application lifecycle** is the path every change takes: plan, build, test, release, then repeat. You never build straight in **production**, the live org your users work in. You build in a **sandbox**, a safe copy of production. Then you test it there and move it over.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A restaurant tries a new dish in a test kitchen first. Diners never taste the experiments. Only the finished recipe goes on the menu. Where it stops: the test kitchen is a separate org, so you need a deployment tool to carry the recipe across.

cards.title: A classic path
items: Build alone in a **Developer sandbox** (no production data)
Combine everyone's work in a Developer Pro sandbox
Run **user acceptance testing** (UAT: real users try it) in a Partial Copy sandbox
Stage the release and train users in a Full sandbox
Release to production, watch it, and start again

cards.title: Change set development
cards.body: In **change set development**, production is the **source of truth**: the one place that holds the real, current version. Admins move setup changes between connected orgs with **change sets**, all with clicks. It suits small teams and simple orgs.

cards.title: Source-driven development
cards.body: In the **org development model**, **source control** is the source of truth. Source control is a shared history of every change, like Git. Teams deploy from it with a **manifest**, a file named `package.xml` that lists what to move. It suits bigger teams who work on the same things.

cards.title: DevOps Center
cards.body: **DevOps Center** (now renamed Lifecycle Center) gives admins source control with clicks. It tracks each change, manages the branches for you and moves work through the release path. No command line needed. Pick it when a team wants source control but works mostly with clicks.

"Just fix it in production, it's faster" is never the exam answer. Untested changes can break live work. And the next release from a sandbox can quietly overwrite that fix, because the sandbox never had it.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Build in a box, test in a box, ship to the house.** Few admins and simple org: change sets. Big team, same files: source control.

terms.say: The steps every change goes through: plan it, build it, test it, release it. Then you start again with the next change.
The real, live org where your users do their daily work. Mistakes here hurt real people, so you don't experiment here.
A safe copy of your production org. You can build and break things there, and production never feels it.
The smallest sandbox. It copies your setup but none of your records, so you can build something by yourself.
Real users try the new feature before it goes live. They check it really does what they asked for.
The one place everyone trusts to hold the real, latest version of something.
Bundles of setup changes you send between your production org and its sandboxes, using only clicks.
A shared history of every change to your files, like Git. You can see who changed what and go back to older versions.
A list of the parts you want to deploy. In Salesforce it's a file called package.xml.
A Salesforce tool for moving changes with clicks while it keeps them in source control for you. Its newer name is Lifecycle Center.

lessons.title: Sandbox types: which one when
lessons.objective: Given a set of business requirements, recommend a solution for managing the application lifecycle, including sandbox types.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **sandbox** is a copy of your production org in a separate place. It's fully isolated: nothing you do there touches production. There are four types. They differ in how much data they copy, how much they can hold, and how often you can **refresh** them (copy production again).

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Practice rooms for a band. A tiny room for one player and a bigger one for a few. Then a hall with part of the audience, and a full copy of the concert stage. Where it stops: a refresh wipes the room and rebuilds it from today's production.

cards.title: Metadata or data?
cards.body: **Metadata** is your setup: objects, fields, page layouts, flows. **Data** means the records, like accounts and cases. Every sandbox copies all of the metadata. Only Partial Copy and Full sandboxes also copy records.

cards.title: The four types
items: **Developer sandbox**: metadata only, 200 MB data, refresh every 1 day
**Developer Pro sandbox**: metadata only, 1 GB data, refresh every 1 day
**Partial Copy sandbox**: metadata plus sample data, 5 GB data, refresh every 5 days
**Full sandbox**: metadata and all data, same storage as production, refresh every 29 days

cards.title: Sandbox templates
cards.body: A **sandbox template** picks which objects' records get copied. A Partial Copy sandbox **requires** one. A Full sandbox can use one to copy less, or copy everything. Developer and Developer Pro sandboxes can't use templates, because they copy no records.

cards.title: Which one when
cards.body: Build and test alone: Developer or Developer Pro. Test with realistic sample records, or run UAT: Partial Copy. Load testing, final staging and training: Full, the only type with all of production's data.

Need every production record? Only a **Full sandbox** has them. Partial Copy holds a sample picked by a template. And Developer Pro has more storage than Developer, but still copies no records at all.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **1, 1, 5, 29.** Developer, Developer Pro, Partial Copy, Full. The more a sandbox copies, the longer you wait between refreshes.

terms.say: A safe copy of your production org. You can build and break things there, and production never feels it.
Throwing away a sandbox's contents and copying production into it again, so it matches today's setup.
Your setup: the objects, fields, layouts and flows. It's the shape of your org, not the records inside it.
The records people save, like each account, contact or case.
The smallest sandbox: setup only, no records, 200 MB of space. You can refresh it every day.
Like a Developer sandbox, but with 1 GB of space. Still setup only, no records. Refresh every day.
A sandbox with your setup plus a sample of records picked by a template. You can refresh it every 5 days.
A complete copy of production: all setup and all records. You can refresh it only every 29 days.
A list of which objects' records to copy into a sandbox. Partial Copy needs one; Full can use one.

lessons.title: Change sets: send and receive
lessons.objective: Given a use case, demonstrate knowledge, viability, and troubleshooting when using change sets.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **change set** is a bundle of setup changes that you send from one org to another, all with clicks. You build an **outbound change set** in the org that has the changes and upload it. The other org sees it as an **inbound change set** and deploys it.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Mail between branches of one company. One branch packs a box and sends it. The other branch receives it and unpacks it. You can't mail it to a different company. Where it stops: the box holds setup only, never records.

cards.title: Deployment connections
cards.body: Change sets only travel between orgs tied to the same production org: production and its sandboxes. A **deployment connection** links each pair automatically. But an admin in the **target org** (the one receiving) must authorize it to accept inbound changes first. That keeps changes on an approved path.

cards.title: The steps
items: In the target org: authorize the connection for inbound changes
In the source org: create the outbound change set and add components
Add the dependent components it needs
Upload it to the target org
In the target org: validate it (optional), then deploy

cards.title: What travels
cards.body: Change sets move **metadata** only: custom objects, fields, page layouts, flows, permission sets and more. They never move records. Load records with a data tool such as **Data Loader**. An inbound change set **deploys as a whole**: you can't pick single components.

cards.title: Who can do it
cards.body: To build and send: the **Create and Upload Change Sets** permission. To receive: **Deploy Change Sets** plus **Modify Metadata Through Metadata API Functions**. Different steps, different permissions.

Two separate companies, each with its own production org? Change sets can't connect them, even with authorization. They only link orgs from the same production org. Use a package or the Metadata API instead.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Pack it out, unpack it in.** Outbound in the source, inbound in the target. The target says yes first.

terms.say: A box of setup changes, sent with clicks from one org to a related org, like a sandbox to production.
The change set you build and send from the org that has the new changes.
A change set that arrived in your org. You can check it, test it and then deploy it.
The link between two related orgs that lets change sets travel. Each org must allow incoming changes.
The org that receives the changes.
Your setup: objects, fields, layouts and flows. It's the shape of your org, not the records inside it.
A Salesforce tool for loading, updating or exporting lots of records at once.
You deploy every part of the change set together. You can't pick only some parts.
A permission that lets a user deploy change sets that arrived in their org.

lessons.title: When change sets fail
lessons.objective: Given a use case, demonstrate knowledge, viability, and troubleshooting when using change sets.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Most change set problems come from two things. Something the change needs is missing. Or you asked a change set to do something it simply can't. Learn both lists and you can fix almost any failure.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Flat-pack furniture. If the box is missing the screws, you can't build the shelf. Where it stops: Salesforce checks the whole box first. If one part fails, it builds nothing at all.

cards.title: Dependencies
cards.body: Add every **dependent component** the target doesn't already have: a flow's fields, a layout's fields, a field's object. Watch out: adding only a custom object deploys it **without its fields**. It doesn't fail, it's just empty. Use View/Add Dependencies to find what's missing.

cards.title: All or nothing
cards.body: A deployment is **one transaction**. If any part fails, the whole thing **rolls back** and nothing changes. Once it succeeds, it can't be rolled back. To undo it, make a new change. A failed deployment also doesn't restart by itself.

cards.title: What change sets can't do
items: Delete or rename components (do it by hand in the target)
Include **standard objects**, so no action overrides on them
Change after upload: **clone** it, add parts, upload again
Hold more than **10,000 files** (split it up)
Move records

cards.title: Validate and tests
cards.body: **Validate** is a test deployment: you see the errors without changing anything. The org is locked for setup changes while it runs, but people can still read and save records. Deploying Apex to production runs all **local tests** and needs 75% **code coverage**. Sandbox targets don't run tests automatically.
"Open the uploaded change set and add the missing field." You can't. An uploaded change set is locked. Clone it, add the field and upload the clone.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Clone to add, delete by hand, validate before you land.**

terms.say: A part that another part needs to work. A flow that uses a field needs that field to arrive too.
One all-or-nothing step. Either every part succeeds, or none of it counts.
Undoes everything from a failed step, so the org looks exactly as it did before.
Objects Salesforce gives you, like Account or Case. Change sets can't carry the object itself.
Make a copy of the change set that you can still edit, then add what was missing.
The most files one change set can hold. Bigger releases must be split into more change sets.
A practice deployment. It shows what would fail, but changes nothing in the org.
The Apex tests that live in your org, not the ones inside installed managed packages.
How much of your Apex code the tests actually run. Production needs at least 75%.

lessons.title: Unmanaged vs managed packages
lessons.objective: Describe the use cases and considerations when using unmanaged and managed packages.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **package** is a container of setup parts you can install in another org, even one you have no connection to. That's how AgentExchange apps reach you. AgentExchange is Salesforce's app marketplace, once called AppExchange. The two classic kinds are unmanaged and managed.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: An unmanaged package is a printed recipe. You can change it any way you like, but the chef can't update your copy. A managed package is a sealed appliance that gets updates from its maker. Where it stops: you can still set up a managed app, like assigning its permission sets.

cards.title: Unmanaged packages
cards.body: An **unmanaged package** gives you parts you can edit freely. They **count** against your org's app, tab and object limits. The provider can't upgrade them. To get a new version, you **uninstall** it and install the new one. Good for templates, samples and one-time sharing.

cards.title: Managed packages
cards.body: A **managed package** hides its code and metadata: you can't see or change them. The provider can **upgrade** it for you. Its contents **don't count** against your app, tab and object limits. Its parts carry a **namespace prefix**, a unique tag like `acme__`. Most AgentExchange apps are managed.

cards.title: Side by side
cards.code:
Unmanaged             Managed
Edit the parts     Yes                   No
See the code       Yes                   No
Get new versions   Uninstall, reinstall  Provider upgrades it
Counts on limits   Yes                   No
cards.body: Read it as: unmanaged is yours to change, managed stays the provider's.

"We want the vendor's fixes to arrive automatically" points to managed. "We need to change the code ourselves" points to unmanaged. A managed package won't let you edit its code, and an unmanaged one never gets upgrades.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Managed = Maintained by the maker.** **Unmanaged = yoU maintain it.**

terms.say: A box of setup parts, like objects, flows and code, that you can install into another org.
Salesforce's online store of apps and parts you can install. It used to be called AppExchange.
A package whose parts become yours to edit. It never gets upgrades from the maker.
Remove an installed package and its parts from your org.
A package the maker keeps control of. You can't change its code, and the maker can send upgrades.
Install a newer version over the old one, keeping your org's setup of it.
Caps on how many apps, tabs and objects your org may have.
A short, unique tag added to a managed package's parts, like acme__. It shows who they belong to.

lessons.title: Unlocked and 2GP packages; installing
lessons.objective: Describe the use cases and considerations when using unmanaged and managed packages.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Newer packages are built from source control with the **Salesforce CLI**, a command-line tool. An **unlocked package** is for your own company's apps. A **second-generation managed package** (2GP) is for apps you sell or share with other companies.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: An unlocked package is your store's own house brand: staff can tweak it on the shelf, but the next delivery replaces the tweaks. A managed 2GP is a sealed brand product shipped to other stores. Where it stops: both get new versions as upgrades.

cards.title: Unlocked packages
cards.body: Unlocked packages split your org's setup into tidy modules. Each **version** is a fixed snapshot you can install as an upgrade. Admins **can change** an unlocked package's metadata in production, for example in an emergency. But the next version can overwrite that change, so add it to source control too.

cards.title: Managed 2GP
cards.body: For new apps you distribute, Salesforce recommends **2GP** over **first-generation** (1GP) managed packages. 2GP is source-driven and built with the Salesforce CLI. A managed package's **namespace** can't change once it's set.

cards.title: Installing a package
items: Test it first in a sandbox or a **Developer Edition** org, never straight in production
Choose who gets it: **Admins Only**, All Users or Specific Profiles (unsure? Admins Only)
If it has Apex, its tests and your org's tests run
Assign its permission sets to the users who need them

cards.body: A managed package's **permission set** is almost right, so you edit it? You can't. Permission sets inside a managed package are locked. Clone it, or make your own, and assign that.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Unlocked = Us. Managed = Market.** Unlocked for your own apps, managed for apps that go out to others.

terms.say: A tool you type commands into. Developers use it to build packages and move setup between orgs.
A package for your own company's apps. Admins can still change its parts after it's installed.
The newer kind of managed package, built from source control with the Salesforce CLI.
One fixed snapshot of a package. A newer version can be installed as an upgrade.
The older kind of managed package, built inside a special org. Salesforce suggests 2GP for new apps.
A short, unique tag on a managed package's parts that shows who made them. It can't change once set.
A free Salesforce org for building and trying things. It isn't connected to your production org.
An install choice that gives the new package only to admins, so others don't see it before it's ready.
A bundle of extra access you can give to users, on top of their profile.

lessons.title: Choosing a deployment plan
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, determine the appropriate deployment plan.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **deployment plan** is your checklist for getting changes into production safely. It says what goes, which tool moves it, when it moves, and what you must do by hand afterward. A good plan means no surprises on release day.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Moving house. You label the boxes, check the truck is big enough, move on a quiet day, then set up the internet by hand. Where it stops: if one box won't fit, the whole move is cancelled, because deployments are all or nothing.

cards.title: A solid plan
items: Build and test in sandboxes, ending with UAT
Include every dependency, plus profiles or permission sets
**Validate** first, ahead of the release window
Deploy in **low-use hours**, away from **maintenance windows**
Do the **post-deploy steps** by hand: records, deletes, renames
Tell users and train them

cards.title: Pick the tool
cards.body: **Change sets**: simple releases between production and its sandboxes. **Packages**: modular apps, or apps for unrelated orgs. **Salesforce CLI** or the **Metadata API**: source control and scripted, repeatable deployments. **DevOps Center**: source control with clicks.

cards.title: A tiny release plan
cards.code:
Release 4.2
1. Build in Developer sandboxes
2. UAT in Partial Copy sandbox "uat"
3. Validate change set in production: Wednesday
4. Deploy: Saturday 7 am (low use)
5. By hand: delete old field, load new records
cards.body: Validate early, deploy when few people work, and list the by-hand jobs.
"We'll roll it back if something breaks" isn't a plan. A finished deployment can't be rolled back. Validate first, and keep a fix ready to deploy instead.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Build, test, validate, deploy, then do the by-hand bits.**

terms.say: A checklist for moving changes into production safely: what moves, how, when, and what to do after.
User acceptance testing: real users try the change before it goes live.
A practice deployment. It shows what would fail, but changes nothing.
Times when few people use the org, like early weekend mornings.
Planned times when Salesforce updates its systems. Some deployment steps don't work then.
Jobs you do by hand after a deployment, like loading records or deleting an old field.
Boxes of setup parts you can install in other orgs, even ones you aren't connected to.
The way tools talk to Salesforce to read and deploy setup, used by the Salesforce CLI.
A Salesforce tool for moving changes with clicks while it keeps them in source control. Its newer name is Lifecycle Center.
A tool you type commands into to move setup between orgs and build packages.

flashcards.front: Why don't you build changes directly in production?
flashcards.back: Production is the live org people work in. Untested changes can break their work. Build in a sandbox, test, then deploy.

flashcards.front: What is the source of truth in change set development?
flashcards.back: Production. Changes move between production and its sandboxes with change sets. In the org development model, source control is the source of truth instead.

flashcards.front: What does DevOps Center give an admin team?
flashcards.back: Click-based releases backed by source control. It tracks changes and manages branches for you. It's now called Lifecycle Center.

flashcards.front: What are the refresh intervals of the four sandbox types?
flashcards.back: Developer: 1 day. Developer Pro: 1 day. Partial Copy: 5 days. Full: 29 days.

flashcards.front: Which sandboxes copy records, not just metadata?
flashcards.back: Only Partial Copy (a sample, picked by a required sandbox template) and Full (all data, template optional). Developer and Developer Pro copy metadata only.

flashcards.front: How much data can Developer and Developer Pro sandboxes hold?
flashcards.back: Developer: 200 MB data and 200 MB files. Developer Pro: 1 GB data and 1 GB files. Both copy metadata only.

flashcards.front: Which sandbox fits load testing, staging and training?
flashcards.back: A Full sandbox. It copies all production data and metadata, and has the same storage as production.

flashcards.front: Between which orgs can change sets travel?
flashcards.back: Only orgs tied to the same production org: production and its sandboxes. Never between unrelated orgs.

flashcards.front: Who must authorize a deployment connection?
flashcards.back: An admin in the receiving (target) org, so it accepts inbound changes from that org.

flashcards.front: Can a change set move records?
flashcards.back: No. Change sets move metadata only. Load records with a data tool such as Data Loader.

flashcards.front: Which permissions deploy an inbound change set?
flashcards.back: Deploy Change Sets plus Modify Metadata Through Metadata API Functions. Creating and sending needs Create and Upload Change Sets.

flashcards.front: How do you add a missing part to an uploaded change set?
flashcards.back: You can't edit it. Clone the change set, add the missing component, then upload the clone.

flashcards.front: What happens when one component in a change set fails to deploy?
flashcards.back: Everything rolls back. A deployment is one transaction: all or nothing. A finished deployment can't be rolled back.

flashcards.front: What does Validate do on an inbound change set?
flashcards.back: It runs a test deployment and shows the results, changing nothing. Setup changes are locked while it runs; records can still be edited.

flashcards.front: Which jobs can a change set never do?
flashcards.back: Delete or rename components, include standard objects, move records, or hold more than 10,000 files.

flashcards.front: How do you get a new version of an unmanaged package?
flashcards.back: Uninstall it, then install the new version. The provider can't upgrade it for you.

flashcards.front: Do managed package objects count against your org's limits?
flashcards.back: No. Managed package contents don't count against app, tab and object limits. Unmanaged package contents do.

flashcards.front: Can you edit the code in a managed package?
flashcards.back: No. You can't see or change its code or metadata. The provider owns it and can upgrade it.

flashcards.front: What is an unlocked package for?
flashcards.back: Your own company's apps, built from source control. It's versioned and upgradeable, and admins can still change its metadata in production.

flashcards.front: Which managed package type does Salesforce recommend for new apps?
flashcards.back: Second-generation managed packages (2GP), built with the Salesforce CLI. Their namespace can't change once set.

flashcards.front: What runs when you install a package with Apex?
flashcards.back: The package's tests and all of your org's tests. You can choose to install even if some fail.

flashcards.front: Can you edit a permission set from a managed package?
flashcards.back: No. Clone it, or create your own. Your clones aren't changed by package upgrades.

flashcards.front: When should a big release be deployed?
flashcards.back: In low-use hours, planned around maintenance windows for both production and sandboxes.

flashcards.front: What goes on the by-hand list after a change set deploys?
flashcards.back: Anything change sets can't do: loading records, deleting or renaming components, and other manual setup.

flashcards.front: Which tool fits a team that uses source control and wants scripted deployments?
flashcards.back: The Salesforce CLI with the Metadata API. Change sets are manual and don't use source control.

questions.q: An admin at Harbor Bikes must add a new field and a flow. Users work in the org all day. Where should the admin build and test the change first?
options: In production during low-use hours, so few users notice
In production, with the field hidden by field-level security
In a sandbox, then deploy it to production after testing
In a Developer Edition org, then send it by change set
questions.explain: Changes are built and tested in a sandbox, a safe copy of production. Only tested work is deployed to the live org.
wrong: Building in production skips testing, whatever the hour.
Hiding a field doesn't make an untested flow safe.
A Developer Edition org isn't tied to production, so change sets can't connect them.

questions.q: In the org development model, what job does source control do?
options: It keeps a shared history of every change and is the source of truth
It copies production records into a sandbox for testing
It locks production so nobody can make setup changes
It moves changes between orgs with no other tool needed
questions.explain: Source control keeps every change in one shared history. In the org development model it is the source of truth, not production.
wrong: Copying records is what a sandbox refresh or template does.
Source control stores changes. It doesn't lock any org.
A deployment tool, like the Salesforce CLI, still moves the changes.

questions.q: Northwind Clinics has two admins who make every change with clicks. The org is simple, and they release a few times a year. Which development approach fits best?
options: Package development with second-generation managed packages
Org development with Git and command-line deployments
Building straight in production after business hours
Change set development, with production as the source of truth
questions.explain: Change sets fit small, clicks-only teams with simple orgs. Source-driven models pay off for bigger teams working on the same things.
wrong: Managed packages are for apps you distribute to other companies.
It works, but adds command-line tools this small team doesn't need.
Building in production skips testing and risks live work.

questions.q: Which two statements describe the org development model? (Choose 2)
options: Changes move between orgs only with change sets
Source control, not production, is the source of truth
Production is the source of truth for every change
Changes are deployed with a manifest such as `package.xml`
Every change must be shipped as a managed package
questions.explain: In the org development model, source control holds the truth. Teams deploy from it with a manifest that lists what to move.
wrong: That describes change set development.
That's also change set development. Here source control holds the truth.
Packages belong to the package development model, and managed ones are for distribution.

questions.q: A team plans this path for every change. Developers need more storage than a Developer sandbox, but no production records. Which sandbox type fits step 2?
questions.code:
1. Build alone:        Developer sandbox
2. Combine all work:   ?
3. UAT:                Partial Copy sandbox
4. Stage and train:    Full sandbox
5. Release:            production
options: Full sandbox
Developer Pro sandbox
Partial Copy sandbox
A second production org
questions.explain: Developer Pro sandboxes copy metadata only and hold 1 GB of data. That fits combining everyone's work without production records.
wrong: Full copies all production data, which this step doesn't need, and refreshes only every 29 days.
Partial Copy copies sample production records, which this step doesn't need. The plan uses it for UAT.
Work is combined in a sandbox, never in another production org.

questions.q: Lakeside Insurance has five admins and two developers. Changes keep overwriting each other, so the team wants every change tracked in source control. Most admins never use a command line. Which tool fits best?
options: Change sets between the team's sandboxes
DevOps Center
The Salesforce CLI with one manifest per admin
Unmanaged packages built in production
questions.explain: DevOps Center gives click-based releases backed by source control. It suits admins who want tracking without a command line. Its newer name is Lifecycle Center.
wrong: Change sets don't use source control, so overwrites stay hidden.
It tracks changes, but needs the command line these admins don't use.
Unmanaged packages can't be upgraded and don't track changes.
questions.source: Trailhead: Lifecycle Center: Centralize DevOps Change Management

questions.q: At Pine Ridge Foods, an admin fixed a validation rule straight in production. A week later, a release from the team's sandbox overwrote the fix. Which practice would have prevented this?
questions.code:
Mon  Admin edits rule in production
     (sandbox still has the old rule)
Sat  Release deployed from sandbox
     -> old rule is back
options: Validating the change set before deploying it
Deploying every release on a weekend morning
Assigning the admin a muting permission set
Making the fix in a sandbox first
questions.explain: Every change should follow the same path from sandbox to production. A fix made only in production is missing from the sandbox, so the next release overwrites it.
wrong: Validation checks that the release deploys. It doesn't spot an untracked fix.
The release time doesn't stop it from overwriting the fix.
Muting permission sets turn off permissions in a group. They don't protect metadata.

questions.q: Copper Kettle is planning the lifecycle for a new app. Which two steps belong in a sound plan? (Choose 2)
options: Let real users test it in a sandbox before release
Run user acceptance testing in production, then delete the test records
Skip sandbox testing for changes made only with clicks
Build every change in a Full sandbox, since it refreshes daily
Train users in a sandbox that matches production
questions.explain: Test and train in sandboxes before anything reaches production. User acceptance testing and training both happen there.
wrong: Testing in production risks real data and live users.
Click changes can break things too, so they get tested.
Full sandboxes refresh every 29 days, not daily.

questions.q: Which sandbox type copies all of production's data?
options: Full
Partial Copy
Developer Pro
Developer
questions.explain: Only a Full sandbox copies all production data, plus all metadata.
wrong: Partial Copy copies only a sample, picked by a sandbox template.
Developer Pro copies metadata only.
Developer copies metadata only.
questions.source: Sandbox Licenses and Storage Limits by Type

questions.q: How often can a Developer sandbox be refreshed?
options: Every 5 days
Every 29 days
Once a day
Every 7 days
questions.explain: Developer and Developer Pro sandboxes can be refreshed every day.
wrong: 5 days is the Partial Copy interval.
29 days is the Full sandbox interval.

questions.q: What can a change set move from a sandbox to production?

questions.q: Harbor Hotels has production, a Dev sandbox and a QA sandbox. Every connection is authorized. Which two change set paths are possible? (Choose 2)

questions.q: Juniper Health's admin created a custom object in QA, with its fields and 30 records of reference data. She deploys a change set with the object and fields. What does production have afterward?

questions.q: An admin can create and upload outbound change sets. In production, she gets a permissions error when she tries to deploy an inbound one. Which two permissions does she need there? (Choose 2)

Manage Sandboxes
Author Apex

questions.explain: Deploying an inbound change set needs Deploy Change Sets plus Modify Metadata Through Metadata API Functions.

questions.q: This inbound change set is waiting in production. The admin wants to deploy only the 3 flows now and the rest next week. What should she do?

questions.q: Orbit Media was bought by Atlas Group. Each company keeps its own production org. Orbit's admin wants to send custom objects and flows to Atlas's org. What should the admin do?

No connection can exist between orgs of two different productions.

questions.q: An admin uploaded a change set, then noticed a field was missing. How can she add it?
options: Clone the change set, add the field, then upload the clone

Add the field to the inbound change set in the target

questions.q: A change set deployed a new custom object to production. In Object Manager, the object has none of its custom fields. What most likely happened?

questions.explain: Adding only a custom object deploys it without its fields. Each field must be added to the change set too.
wrong: Field-level security controls user access. Object Manager still lists the fields.

Custom fields deploy to production by change set just fine.

questions.q: Which two tasks can't be done with a change set? (Choose 2)

Adding a new page layout to the target org
Renaming a custom object in the target org
Moving a new flow to the target org
Adding a new permission set to the target org

Permission sets can be deployed by change set.
